metadata.methods_description: Data collection involved simultaneous recording of EEG, EOG, ECG, respiration, pupillary responses, gaze coordinates, and head position during two sessions: an attentive condition with post-video comprehension testing (Session 1) and a distracted condition with concurrent backward counting task (Session 2). EEG data were recorded in BDF format; physiological and eye-tracking data were converted to compressed TSV format using MATLAB-based processing pipelines.

citation_details.title: Attentional state, not trait, predicts test performance in video-based learning
citation_details.author: Jens Madsen, Lucas C. Parra
citation_details.abstract: Summary Poor academic performance is often linked to attention deficits, but it remains unclear whether these reflect enduring traits or momentary lapses in focus. In this study, we examined how state and trait-level attention relate to learning from short educational videos. Across four experiments (N = 152), participants completed standardized assessments of inattention, hyperactivity, working memory capacity, and GPA. They then viewed 3-6-minute educational videos while electroencephalography (EEG) tracked neural responses, followed by quizzes assessing short-term retention. Neural synchrony during video viewing, a measure of attentional state, strongly predicted test performance (p < 0.001). In contrast, trait inattention did not predict retention (p > 0.05), although it was negatively associated with GPA. citation_details.title: The Brain, Body, and Behaviour Dataset (1.0.0) - Experiment 4
citation_details.author: Jens Madsen, Nikhil Kuppa, Lucas Parra
citation_details.abstract: The Brain, Body, and Behaviour Dataset (Experiment 4) is a multimodal neurophysiological dataset comprising simultaneous recordings of EEG, eye-tracking, cardiac, respiratory, and electrooculographic signals from 43 subjects across two sessions. Participants watched three educational videos (Stim-04, Stim-05, Stim-06) under two attention conditions. In Session 1 (attentive condition), participants viewed the videos and answered comprehension questions afterward. In Session 2 (distracted condition), participants viewed the same three videos in the same order while performing a concurrent backward counting task, with no comprehension testing. This derivative dataset supports investigation of neural and behavioral correlates of attention, learning, and cognitive load during naturalistic video viewing.

citation_details.author: Tasikala Rathnayake, Subodha Subasingha, Malithi Nawarathne, Prasanna Sumathipala, Vidanaralage A. J.
citation_details.venue: 2026 IEEE International Research Conference on Smart Computing and Systems Engineering (SCSE)
citation_details.abstract: Monitoring learner attention during video-based learning is important for adaptive educational systems. However, common indicators such as clicks, video completion, and quiz scores do not directly reflect whether learners remain attentive. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a noninvasive and time-sensitive measure of brain activity for attention-state assessment. This study investigates whether interpretable EEG spectral features can classify attentive and distracted states during instructional video viewing. EEG recordings from 30 participants in Experiment 2 of the Brain, Body, and Behavior Dataset (BBBD) were analyzed using the common stimulus stim01 under attentive and distracted conditions. The signals were segmented into 4 s windows with 2 s overlap, producing 5278 windows (2730 attentive, 2548 distracted). citation_details.author: Tasikala Rathnayake, Subodha Subasingha, Malithi Nawarathne, Vidanaralage A. J., Prasanna Sumathipala
citation_details.venue: 2026 IEEE International Research Conference on Smart Computing and Systems Engineering (SCSE)
citation_details.abstract: In recent years, video-based learning has emerged as a prominent instructional approach for enhancing learner engagement in digital education. However, sustaining attention in such multimedia environments remains a critical challenge, particularly in the absence of real-time cognitive feedback. Electroencephalography (EEG) has gained increasing attention as a non-invasive neurophysiological tool for objectively assessing attentional states through brainwave patterns associated with cognitive processing. This systematic literature review examines EEG-based attention assessment techniques in video-based learning environments, grounded in Schema Theory, a cognitive framework that emphasizes the role of prior knowledge structures in guiding attention and learning.
